m: A person with a refined appreciation of art and beauty (sometimes excessive).
e: Coined in 19th-century English from Greek aisthētēs, “one who perceives”, from aisthanesthai (to perceive, feel). Tied to Oscar Wilde’s Aesthetic movement and “art for art’s sake”.
t: Picture Oscar Wilde with a lily and a velvet jacket. Aesthete = the person; aesthetic = the quality.

m: Concerned with beauty or artistic taste.
e: Greek aisthētikos, “of sense perception”, from aisthanesthai (to perceive). The German philosopher Baumgarten gave it the meaning “theory of taste” in the 1700s.
t: Anesthetic = no feeling. Aesthetic = what your senses feel, especially beauty.

m: Showing no interest, enthusiasm or concern.
e: Greek apatheia: a- (without) + pathos (feeling, suffering). For the Stoics apatheia was an ideal; in English it became indifference.
t: A-pathos = no feeling, the opposite of sympathy and passion. Same as French apathique.

m: Bold and daring; sometimes shamelessly so.
e: Latin audax, audacis (bold), from audere (to dare).
t: Danton in 1792: « De l’audace, encore de l’audace, toujours de l’audace ! » Audacious can praise or condemn.

m: Lacking originality; trite.
e: French banal, from the feudal ban (the lord’s jurisdiction; a Frankish word). The four banal and moulin banal were the lord’s oven and mill every villager had to use: “common to all” became “commonplace”.
t: Picture the village four banal: everyone bakes in the same oven, so every loaf looks the same.

m: Relating to the pleasant side of country life; pastoral.
e: Greek boukolikos, “of herdsmen”, from boukolos (cowherd): bous (ox) + -kolos (tending). Virgil’s Bucolics made it a literary genre.
t: Bous = ox. A cowherd lounging in a meadow, Virgil-style. Same as French bucolique.

m: To laugh in a gleeful, breathy way.
e: Coined by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871) as a blend of chuckle + snort.
t: Chuckle + snort = chortle. The satisfied, slightly smug laugh after winning an argument.

m: To admit something is true, often reluctantly; to yield.
e: Latin concedere, “to give way”: com- + cedere (to go, yield).
t: Concéder: same word. You concede a point in an argument, or concede defeat in an election.

m: Clearly visible; attracting attention.
e: Latin conspicuus (visible), from conspicere, “to look at closely”: com- + specere (to look), the root of spectacle and perspicace.
t: Veblen’s “conspicuous consumption” (1899): the logo-covered handbag bought to be seen. Conspicuous = made to be looked at.

m: Mysterious; obscure in meaning.
e: Late Latin crypticus, from Greek kryptikos, from kryptos (hidden). Same root as crypt and cryptography.
t: Kryptos = hidden, like a crypt under a church. A cryptic message keeps its meaning underground.

m: To reach the highest point or climax.
e: Late Latin culminare (to crown), from culmen (summit). Astronomers used it for a star reaching its highest point in the sky.
t: « Le point culminant » = the summit. A career that culminates in the CEO role reaches its peak there.

m: Responsibility for a fault or wrong; blameworthiness.
e: Latin culpabilis (blameworthy), from culpa (fault, blame).
t: Mea culpa = my fault. Culpability = culpabilité.

m: In keeping with good taste and propriety; polite.
e: Latin decorus (becoming, proper), from decor (seemliness), from decere (to be fitting). Same root as decorum and décent.
t: Think « le décorum »: decorous behaviour respects decorum. Nothing to do with decorations.

m: Showing respect and humble submission.
e: From deference, French déférence, from déférer (to yield to), Latin deferre: de- + ferre (to carry).
t: Same as « par déférence ». A deferential junior defers to the partner’s judgment.

m: Domineering; imposing one’s will on others.
e: Latin dictator, from dictare (to say repeatedly, prescribe). In Rome a dictator was a magistrate given absolute power for six months in an emergency.
t: The one who dictates. A dictatorial manager dictates and nobody else gets to speak.

m: Intended to teach, often in a preachy or moralising way.
e: Greek didaktikos, “apt at teaching”, from didaskein (to teach).
t: Same as « didactique ». On the GRE it often stings a little: a didactic novel lectures you.

m: Shy; lacking self-confidence.
e: Latin diffidentem, from diffidere, “to mistrust”: dis- (not) + fidere (to trust), as in fidèle and confiance. First it meant distrusting others; now, distrusting yourself.
t: Dis + fidere = no trust. Défiance is mistrust of others; diffidence is mistrust of yourself. Opposite: confident (con + fidere).

m: Asserting opinions as undeniably true; inflexible.
e: Greek dogmatikos, from dogma (opinion, decree), from dokein (to seem, think).
t: Dogma = a decree that can’t be questioned. Same as French dogmatique.

m: To cause or give rise to.
e: Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerare: in- + generare (to beget), from genus (birth, kind).
t: Same as « engendrer ». A policy engenders resentment the way parents engender children.

m: Firmly established and hard to change.
e: en- + trench, from Old French trenche (a cut, a ditch), from trenchier (now trancher), probably from Latin truncare (to cut off).
t: Picture WWI soldiers dug into their tranchées for years. An entrenched belief is dug in and won’t move.

m: To deliberately avoid; abstain from.
e: Old French eschiver (later esquiver), from Frankish skiuhan (to fear, shun). A cousin of English shy and German scheuen.
t: Eschew = esquiver. Say it “es-CHOO” and picture dodging a sneeze. To eschew meat = to avoid it on principle.

m: To make a problem worse.
e: Latin exacerbare (to irritate, make harsh): ex- + acerbus (harsh, bitter).
t: Acerbus = acerbe. Pouring something bitter on a wound: same as « exacerber ».

m: Happening by chance (not necessarily lucky).
e: Latin fortuitus (happening by chance), from fors (chance), the root of Fortuna.
t: « Une rencontre fortuite » = a chance meeting. On the GRE, fortuitous means accidental, not fortunate.

m: Not serious; silly, trivial.
e: Latin frivolus (silly, empty, worthless), possibly from friare (to crumble).
t: Identical to frivole. Things that crumble into nothing: a frivolous lawsuit has no substance.

m: To deny or contradict.
e: Middle English: gain-, “against” (Old English gegn, as in again and against) + say. Purely Germanic.
t: Gain = against: to say against. “No one can gainsay her results” = no one can contradict them.

m: Bold, impudent behaviour; nerve. (Also bitterness, bile.)
e: Old English gealla (bile), from an Indo-European root for yellow-green; related to Greek cholē (bile, as in cholera and mélancolie). Bitterness became audacity in 19th-century American slang.
t: The gall bladder holds bitter bile. Having the gall to ask = avoir le culot. To gall someone = to irritate them.

m: Relevant to the subject at hand.
e: A variant of german, “of the same parents”, from Latin germanus (full brother or sister). Closely related, hence relevant.
t: Cousin germain! A germane point is closely related to the topic, like a first cousin.

m: An excessive supply; to oversupply.
e: Middle English glotten (to swallow greedily), from Old French gloutir, from Latin gluttire (to swallow). Same root as glouton and engloutir.
t: Glouton + engloutir: a market so stuffed it can’t swallow any more. A glut of oil = prices collapse.

m: Extremely light, thin and delicate; fine spider silk.
e: Middle English gossomer, probably “goose summer”: the warm spell in late autumn (St Martin’s summer) when geese were eaten and fine cobwebs floated over the fields.
f: fils de la Vierge; arachnéen, vaporeux
t: « Les fils de la Vierge »: threads of spider silk drifting over a field in an Indian summer. Gossamer = that light.

m: Not showing due respect; shamelessly bold.
e: Latin impudentem (shameless): in- (not) + pudens (modest), from pudere (to feel shame).
t: In + pudeur = no shame. Same as French impudent, and close to gall and impertinent.

m: Sharp and clear-thinking; going straight to the point.
e: Medieval Latin incisivus, from incidere, “to cut into”: in- + caedere (to cut).
t: Your incisives are the cutting teeth. An incisive question cuts straight to the core of the problem.

m: Impossible to stop or prevent; relentless.
e: Latin inexorabilis: in- (not) + exorabilis (moved by pleading), from exorare: ex- + orare (to pray, plead; cf. oraison).
t: In-ex-orare = can’t be moved by prayer. Like death or the tide: beg all you want.

m: To criticise harshly.
e: 1630s, probably lam (to beat, from Old Norse lemja) + baste (to thrash). Both halves mean hitting.
t: Lam + baste = beat + beat. A critic who lambasts a film gives it a double thrashing: « se faire éreinter par la critique ».

m: Excessively, sickly sentimental.
e: From mawk (maggot), Old Norse maðkr. In the 1660s it meant “sickly, nauseated”; by the 1700s, “sickly-sweet sentimental”.
f: mièvre, à l’eau de rose, gnangnan
t: Sentimentality so sweet it turns your stomach like maggots. A mawkish Christmas ad = mièvre.

m: Showing great attention to detail; very careful.
e: Latin meticulosus (fearful, timid), from metus (fear). In 19th-century French, méticuleux shifted to “afraid of making mistakes”, hence careful.
t: Same as méticuleux. Metus = fear: a meticulous person is scared of making a single mistake.

m: To make less severe or painful.
e: Latin mitigare (to soften): mitis (mild, gentle) + agere (to make).
t: Mitigating circumstances = « circonstances atténuantes ». Mitis = soft: you soften the blow.

m: Not well known, or unclear; to conceal.
e: Latin obscurus (dark, dim, hidden).
t: Identical to obscur. Something in the dark is either unknown or hard to see clearly.

m: Deceitfulness; treachery.
e: Latin perfidia (faithlessness): per- (away, to ruin) + fides (faith).
t: « La perfide Albion »: the classic French jab at England’s supposed treachery. Per + fides = breaking faith.

m: A remark used too often to be interesting; a cliché.
e: French platitude (17th century), “flatness”, from plat (flat), from Vulgar Latin plattus, from Greek platys (broad, flat).
t: Same as « platitude »: a flat, dull remark. “Let’s think outside the box” is a corporate platitude.

m: To prevent from happening; make impossible.
e: Latin praecludere (to shut off in advance): prae- (before) + claudere (to close).
t: Pre + close = closing the door in advance. Same root as exclude and clore.

m: A preference or special liking.
e: French prédilection, from Medieval Latin praedilectio: prae- (before) + diligere (to love, choose).
t: Identical: « un sujet de prédilection ». A predilection for good coffee is a favourite habit.

m: Knowledge of events before they happen; foresight.
e: Latin praescientia: prae- (before) + scire (to know).
t: Pre + science = knowing before. A prescient investor saw the crash coming.

m: Complaining in a whining, petulant way.
e: Latin querulus, from queri (to complain). Same root as querelle and quarrel.
t: Queri → querelle. A querulous person picks small complaints all day long.

m: Little known; obscure; hard to understand.
e: Latin reconditus (hidden, put away), from recondere: re- + condere (to put, store). Its cousin abscondere (to hide away) gave French abscons.
t: Recondite ≈ abscons: knowledge stored away where few can find it, like a footnote in a dusty archive.

m: Not revealing one’s thoughts readily; reserved.
e: Latin reticentem, from reticere (to keep silent): re- + tacere (to be silent), as in taciturne.
t: Tacere = se taire: a reticent person holds back their words. Modern French réticent means reluctant; for the GRE, think taciturn.

m: Of the countryside; simple, unsophisticated.
e: Latin rusticus, from rus (countryside), as in rural.
t: Same as rustique. Rus = countryside: a rustic table is rough wood from the farm.

m: Unnecessary; more than enough.
e: Latin superfluus (overflowing): super (over) + fluere (to flow).
t: Superflu: water overflowing the glass. The extra words on a slide are superfluous.

m: Physical or mental inactivity; lethargy.
e: Latin torpor (numbness), from torpere (to be numb). The Latin torpedo was the electric ray, the fish that numbs its prey.
t: « La torpeur de l’après-midi ». Picture being zapped by a torpille fish: numb and sluggish.

m: Loud and forceful in expressing opinions.
e: Latin vociferari (to shout): vox, vocis (voice) + ferre (to carry).
t: « Vociférer » = to yell. A vociferous critic carries their voice far and loud.

m: Fluent, ready, continuous speech; talkativeness.
e: Latin volubilis (that turns, rolls easily), from volvere (to roll).
t: Words that keep rolling out (volvere). Same as « volubilité ». Opposite of laconic and reticent.
